title: Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers
subcategory: Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers — Acidity, Preparation, Reactions

references.label: NCERT Chemistry Part II, Class 12 — Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers

summary: Phenols are significantly more acidic than alcohols because their conjugate base (phenoxide ion) is resonance-stabilised; alcohols undergo characteristic reactions like dehydration, oxidation and esterification, while ethers are prepared via Williamson synthesis and are comparatively less reactive.
explanation: Phenol (C₆H₅OH) is markedly MORE ACIDIC than a typical alcohol (like ethanol) because its conjugate base, the phenoxide ion, is stabilised by RESONANCE — the negative charge on oxygen delocalises into the aromatic ring, spreading it out and lowering the ion's energy; alcohols lack this resonance stabilisation entirely for their alkoxide conjugate base, which keeps the full negative charge localised on oxygen. Electron-withdrawing substituents (like -NO₂) on the ring further increase phenol's acidity (by additional resonance/inductive stabilisation of the phenoxide), while electron-donating groups (like -OCH₃, alkyl groups) decrease it. The Lucas test distinguishes primary, secondary, and tertiary alcohols by their differing rates of reaction with Lucas reagent (conc. HCl + ZnCl₂, forming a cloudy alkyl chloride via SN1 for more substituted alcohols): tertiary alcohols react immediately (turbidity within minutes, forming the most stable carbocation), secondary alcohols react within about 5-10 minutes (warming may help), and primary alcohols show no visible reaction at room temperature. Alcohols undergo dehydration (loss of water, typically with conc. H₂SO₄ or H₃PO₄ and heat) to form alkenes, following Saytzeff's rule for the major product (more substituted alkene, since it's typically formed via a carbocation intermediate for secondary/tertiary alcohols); they also undergo oxidation, where a PRIMARY alcohol oxidises stepwise to an aldehyde then a carboxylic acid, a SECONDARY alcohol oxidises directly to a ketone (and no further, under normal conditions), and a TERTIARY alcohol resists oxidation entirely (no H atom available on the carbon bearing -OH). Esterification with a carboxylic acid (Fischer esterification, acid-catalysed) forms an ester + water. Ethers are prepared by Williamson ether synthesis: an alkoxide ion (from a sodium alkoxide) performs SN2 attack on a primary alkyl halide/tosylate, forming a new C-O-C ether linkage — this method works best with a PRIMARY halide (to favour SN2 over competing elimination, which becomes a problem with secondary/tertiary halides and a strong, small alkoxide base).
commonMisconceptions: Assuming alcohols and phenols have comparable acidity simply because both have an -OH group — phenol is many orders of magnitude more acidic than a typical alcohol due to resonance stabilisation of the phenoxide ion, an effect alcohols entirely lack.

Expecting a tertiary alcohol to oxidise to a ketone or acid under ordinary oxidation conditions — a tertiary alcohol has NO hydrogen on the carbon bearing -OH, so it cannot be oxidised this way at all under normal conditions.

Trying Williamson synthesis with a bulky/tertiary alkyl halide and expecting good ether yield — this strongly favours competing ELIMINATION instead, since the strong alkoxide base/nucleophile struggles with SN2 on a hindered carbon.
examples: Phenol reacts with aqueous NaOH to form sodium phenoxide (demonstrating its acidity), whereas ethanol does not react with NaOH under similar conditions.
Isopropanol (secondary alcohol) is oxidised by acidified potassium dichromate to acetone (a ketone), stopping there rather than proceeding to a carboxylic acid.
genZNote: Phenoxide spreads the negative charge across the whole ring — that's resonance flexing, and it's why phenol's more acidic.
